standard.title: Groups in Medieval Europe
standard.description: the roles and relationships of different groups in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain the organisation and roles of key groups in ancient society and how they influenced change (AC9HH7K10). They have not yet examined how group roles and relationships were structured in the medieval European context — the feudal hierarchy, the Church as an institution, the emerging merchant classes, and continuity and change in daily life across the period.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the roles and relationships of different groups in Medieval, Renaissance or pre-modern Europe — including the feudal hierarchy, the institutional role of the Church, the emergence of merchant and artisan classes, the experiences of women, and continuities and changes in daily life — and describe how these roles both shaped and reflected the power structures of the period.

nodes.label: The feudal hierarchy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the structure of feudal society — including the roles and responsibilities of the king, nobles, Church, knights, peasants, and men and women — and explain the obligations that structured relationships between them.
nodes.minimum_width: At least three groups in the feudal hierarchy with a description of their roles and the obligations between them.
nodes.typical_width: The full feudal hierarchy with specific roles, rights and obligations at each level; the distinction between secular and religious authority; the differing roles of men and women across social strata.
wider: Compare the feudal hierarchy in different regions of Europe (e.g. England vs the Italian city-states) to see how the model varied in practice and over time
Examine how the feudal hierarchy was justified ideologically through religious and natural order arguments, and why those justifications were eventually contested
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot place groups in the hierarchy and explain the obligations between them cannot make sense of how power was exercised, contested or reformed in subsequent nodes on turning points and power. The hierarchy is the structural scaffold for all group-relationship analysis.

response_modes.reason: Students often reduce feudalism to a flat list of groups. Scaffold the relational logic — each level owes something to levels above and below — and the distinction between land tenure and personal loyalty as organising mechanisms.

success_criteria: Names the main social groups in the feudal hierarchy and describes the obligations that structured their relationships
Distinguishes between at least two groups in terms of their roles and status (e.g. nobility vs clergy, knights vs peasantry)

nodes.label: The role of the Church
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the role of the Church as a social, political and cultural institution in medieval Europe — including its authority over spiritual and everyday life, its provision of education and welfare, and its relationship with secular rulers.
nodes.minimum_width: At least two distinct roles of the Church (e.g. spiritual authority, education, political power) with a brief explanation of why the Church held such influence.
nodes.typical_width: The Church as a parallel power structure to secular feudalism — its hierarchy, economic power (tithes, land), role in literacy and law, provision of social services, and tensions between papal and royal authority.
wider: Examine the role of monasteries as centres of learning, agriculture and community welfare — particularly the preservation of ancient texts — to see how the Church's institutional functions extended beyond religious practice
Investigate a specific Church-state conflict (e.g. the Investiture Controversy) as a case study in how Church and secular authority negotiated power

response_modes.reason: Students tend to limit the Church to religious functions. Varying contexts — education, land ownership, courts, social welfare, illuminated manuscripts — helps them grasp the Church as a multidimensional institution with social and political as well as spiritual authority.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Church as a parallel power structure with its own hierarchy, economy, legal system and social welfare functions is conceptually rich and directly prepares students for the power and authority analysis in AC9HH8K04.
success_criteria: Explains at least two distinct functions of the Church in medieval society (spiritual, educational, political, economic or welfare)
Describes the relationship between Church authority and secular feudal authority, including at least one point of overlap or tension

nodes.label: Continuity and change in daily life
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe continuities and changes in daily life across medieval society in at least one area — such as crime and punishment, towns and commerce, farming and environment — and explain what drove those changes.
nodes.minimum_width: A description of daily life in at least one area (e.g. farming, towns, crime) with one example of continuity and one of change.
nodes.typical_width: Continuities and changes across multiple domains — e.g. the environmental impact of medieval agriculture; the growth of towns; the spread of literacy and new institutions (universities, guilds, coffee houses); the reach of printed books in the later medieval period.
wider: Examine the reactions to the Black Death — including the emergence of flagellants and persecution of Jewish people — as a case study in how crisis drove both change and continuity in medieval society
Investigate daily life in Renaissance Italy — the roles of men and women, the influence of city-state government (e.g. Naples vs Florence) — to show how urban contexts modified social structures

response_modes.reason: Students need sufficient accumulated examples across domains before they can generalise about medieval daily life. One domain is not enough — build range across farming, towns, law and culture before expecting students to draw conclusions about the period.

success_criteria: Describes daily life in at least one area of medieval society with specific reference to the period
Identifies at least one continuity and one change in the chosen area and offers an explanation for what drove the change

nodes.label: Emerging classes and the Scientific Revolution
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the emergence of merchant and artisan classes, the spread of literacy and new ideas, and the contribution of key theories to the Scientific Revolution, and explain how these developments modified medieval social and intellectual structures.
nodes.minimum_width: An explanation of how at least one new class or intellectual development (e.g. merchants, the printing press, Copernicus) changed the social or intellectual landscape of late medieval and early modern Europe.
nodes.typical_width: The emergence of a merchant class and guild system; the growth of universities, scientific academies and debating societies; the contribution of Copernicus, Galileo and Newton to overturning traditional views; the printing press as a vehicle for disseminating new ideas.
wider: Compare the similarities and differences of daily life between the popolo minuto (common people) and popolo grasso (wealthy merchant class) in Renaissance Italy as a lens on class differentiation
Examine how new commodities from trade (e.g. from the Americas and Asia) drove economic change and modified the costs and quality of basic foodstuffs, connecting economic expansion to daily life

response_modes.reason: Students need to see the connection between merchant class growth, the spread of literacy, new institutions and the Scientific Revolution as a chain of enabling conditions — not separate events. Scaffold the logic from economic change to institutional change to intellectual change.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one new social or intellectual development in late medieval or early modern Europe and explains how it modified existing structures
Describes the contribution of at least one key individual or theory to the Scientific Revolution and connects it to broader social change
